newsitem.title: USA: Senate passes bill to store nuke waste in Nevada.
newsitem.headline: Senate passes bill to store nuke waste in Nevada.

text.p: The Senate passed a bill Tuesday that would require the government to build a facility in Nevada to store thousands of tons of nuclear waste from power plants until it has a permanent underground dump ready.

The bill was approved 65-34, two votes short of the number needed to override a threatened presidential veto. But Republicans were confident they would be able to save the bill even if President Clinton blocked it.
"I'm inclined to think we may on a veto override pick up at least one Republican senator," said Alaska Republican Sen. Frank Murkowski, who sponsored the bill.
However, the two Republicans who opposed the bill -- Sen. Ben Nighthorse Campbell of Colorado and Dan Coats of Indiana -- gave no signals that they would reverse their positions.

A spokeswoman for Campbell said "as it stands he remains opposed to this bill." And a spokesman for Coats, who has opposed the legislation twice, said the senator "has not said to anyone whether he would decide to change his mind."

The bill, bitterly opposed by Nevadans, was designed to help utilities that were promised in 1982 that the government would start removing spent fuel from their plants next year to put it all in one underground dump, which is not yet ready.

States and utilities, which have paid more than $8 billion into a federal fund to build a nuclear waste dump, are suing the government to live up to its contract. But even if Congress passes the bill, Murkowski said the government could still face billions of dollars in damages from the lawsuit.

Critics said the legislation, which calls for nuclear waste to be stored above ground at the government's Nevada Test Site starting in 2003, will drain money from the federal project to bury the waste forever in Nevada's Yucca Mountain.

Democrats said it would allow nuclear waste to be hauled across the country from 80 plants to Nevada, where it may end up parked permanently on concrete pads without an underground dump ever being built. The bill "is an environmental nightmare. (It) is a financial and public safety threat to every American," said Sen. Harry Reid, one of Nevada's two Democratic senators who led the fight against the bill.
Reid said the bill did not adequately ensure safe transportation of the waste and would make the radioactive material an easy target for terrorists.

Democrat Sen. Richard Durbin of Illinois, which gets more than half its power from nuclear energy and has more spent fuel accumulated than any other state, said he hoped the bill would eventually address environmental concerns so he could back it.
Utilities want the spent fuel to be taken away as soon as possible because some plants will start running out of storage space next year.
Yucca Mountain is the one site being studied for a permanent dump, which the Energy Department expects to be ready only in 2015, assuming the mountain is found to be safe.

The bill links the move to build a temporary storage facility at the Nevada Test Site to a decision by the Energy Department scheduled to be made in December 1998 on whether nearby Yucca Mountain would be safe for an underground dump.
"There are only two options -- safe, centralized storage, or a continued 41-state pileup of high-level radioactive materials," Murkowski said.
House lawmakers expect similar legislation on their side to move quickly, with enough votes to override a veto.
